home.sparkle_p1: A desktop video editor for people who cut for a living, and the first place those values had to survive contact with a real product. What makes it unusual is not the models — it is that they sit inside the editor rather than beside it. An edit the assistant makes is an edit you could have made by hand, and one undo takes it back.
home.sparkle_p2: Most of its AI runs on the machine the footage is already on, and the generative work that needs the cloud is metered where you can see it. In private preview.
home.next_p1: A product of this kind leaves a great deal behind it that is not the product: accounts and permissions, the services that run the models, the systems that keep the money honest. None of it is interesting, and all of it is what the next product no longer has to build.
home.pull: Spiders do not spin for the pleasure of it. The structure is what makes everything after it possible.
home.next_p2: Sparkle came first because a company is only believable about its second product once it has finished the first. What that took already exists; the next one starts from there.
home.rail_motto_body: The company is named after the German word for spider. A web is not decoration: it is the structure everything else stands on, and it is built one thread at a time.
home.rail_engineering_body: Investors, partners and suppliers usually want to know what is actually underneath. How we build is that page.

sparkle.title: Sparkle — a video editor with an engine under it
sparkle.description: Sparkle is a desktop video editor: GPU rendering, most of the AI on the machine the footage is already on, hardware encoding that adapts to your silicon. In private preview.
sparkle.og_title: A video editor with an engine under it
sparkle.og_description: GPU rendering, most of the AI on your own machine, and hardware encoding that adapts to your silicon.
sparkle.tw_description: The machine takes the labour. You keep the cut.
sparkle.h1: A video editor with an engine under it.
sparkle.lede: Sparkle is a desktop application for people who cut for a living. GPU rendering, AI models that run on your own machine, hardware encoding that adapts to your silicon — and an assistant that never touches your cut without being asked.
sparkle.h2_problem: Most of an edit is not editing
sparkle.problem_p1: Before anybody makes a creative decision, somebody watches the footage end to end, marks the scene changes, groups the takes, cuts the silences, types the subtitles, and gets twelve clips from three cameras to agree on what colour the evening was.
sparkle.problem_p2: Days of it, before the first real decision. None of it the work anyone trained for.
sparkle.problem_p3: Tools that promise to fix this usually fix it by taking the decisions: hand over the footage, receive an edit, hope you agree. Sparkle goes the other way.
sparkle.pull: The machine takes the labour. You keep the cut.
sparkle.preview_p1: Most transitions are shaders that run on the GPU while you scrub — a plain fade, and anything sitting next to a still, take a simpler path. The export runs none of those shaders. It uses the encoder's own transition set, where about ten of ours have a match by name and the rest are approximated to the nearest look it has. The preview is a close guide to the file rather than a promise of it, and transitions are where the two come apart.
sparkle.preview_p2: Heavy footage gets proxies and a scrub path built for long timelines, which is the difference between an editor you can think in and one you wait for.
sparkle.h2_ai: Most of the AI runs on your machine
sparkle.ai_p1: Background removal, subject segmentation and depth estimation run as local models on your own hardware. An afternoon of rushes does not have to be uploaded to become useful, and for this work footage under embargo stays under embargo.
sparkle.ai_p2: Speech to text can run locally too, on a Whisper model the editor fetches once and then runs without a network. Name that model and the audio stays on the machine. Leave the engine on Auto and it goes to a cloud engine whenever one is configured, at any length — so where your audio goes is a setting, and it is one worth setting.
sparkle.ai_p3: Masks track across frames using optical flow rather than being redrawn shot by shot. Captions arrive with word-level timing, so they can be styled, re-cut and exported to the formats the rest of the industry expects.
sparkle.ai_p4: The heavier generative work needs the cloud, and that part is metered where you can see it. Every account holds a balance of credits; an operation reserves what it might cost before it starts and settles for what it actually cost. Nobody discovers a bill at the end of the month.
sparkle.h2_export: Export that talks to your hardware
sparkle.export_p1: Encoding uses whatever accelerator it finds — NVIDIA NVENC, Intel Quick Sync, AMD, Apple VideoToolbox — and drops to x264, x265 or SVT-AV1 in software when there is nothing to talk to. H.264, HEVC, AV1 and DNxHR for the edit suite, with HDR handled rather than flattened.
sparkle.export_p2: Colour goes through a 3D LUT pipeline, so a look built elsewhere arrives intact. Audio can be loudness-normalised on the way out — a measurement pass to a -14 LUFS master — because a delivery that fails loudness spec is a delivery you make twice. It is a checkbox rather than a default, so it is worth finding once.
sparkle.who_p1: Editors and small post-production teams — people who live in a timeline and notice every hour the software gives back. The desktop editor is free. Cloud AI is billed per member of your organisation, so three editors pay for three rather than a licence tier somebody invented. There is no idle rate: a member who never opens the editor costs the same as one who edits daily. The credit balance above is how the cloud work on an account is metered.
sparkle.status_p1: Sparkle is in private preview. Editor, cloud services, accounts and billing are built and running; access opens gradually, because software that handles other people's footage and other people's money deserves to be let out slowly. If you cut for a living and want in, write and say what you cut.

sparkle.rail_short_body: It does not take the edit off you. The assistant does not touch a cut it was not asked to touch, and it cannot do anything the editor itself cannot do — which is the reason a single undo takes any of it back.

how_we_build.title: Where the editor ends and the model begins — Spinne Software
how_we_build.description: How Sparkle is built: one document, one set of operations on it, and an assistant that is another caller rather than another program.
how_we_build.og_title: Where the editor ends and the model begins
how_we_build.og_description: In most tools there is a seam between the editor and the AI. This is what it took to remove it.
how_we_build.tw_description: The model is the easy part. Everything around it is the editor.
how_we_build.h1: Where the editor ends and the model begins.
how_we_build.lede: In most tools there is a seam. You export, you upload, you wait, you download, you put the result back and hope it still lines up. On one side of that seam is your project; on the other is a program that has never heard of it. Sparkle does not have the seam, and removing it is most of the engineering on this page.
how_we_build.h2_document: An editor is a document and the operations that change it
how_we_build.document_p1: Underneath the panels, an editor is one thing: a document describing what happens when, and a set of named operations that are the only way to change it. Split a clip, retime it, set a colour, add a caption track. Nothing else touches the document.
how_we_build.document_p2: That sounds like an implementation detail and it is the whole architecture. Once the operations are the only door, everything that matters later — undo, concurrency, replay, an audit of what happened — is a property of the door rather than something bolted onto each feature that walks through it.
how_we_build.h2_caller: So the assistant is another caller, not another program
how_we_build.caller_p1: The assistant does not generate code, and it does not generate frames. It emits the same named operations a menu item emits, with the same typed parameters, into the same document. Ask it to cut a vertical version and it calls the operation the editor already had.
how_we_build.caller_p2: Two things follow, and both are the point. It cannot express anything the editor cannot do, so there is no category of AI output that has to be reconciled with the project afterwards. And anything it did, you could have done — which means you can read it, change it, or take it apart by hand.
how_we_build.undo_p1: An assistant operation can touch a hundred clips: retime them, recolour them, restyle every caption. It still collapses to a single checkpoint, so one undo puts you back to before you asked.
how_we_build.undo_p2: This is not a convenience. What makes an editing assistant usable is not how often it is right — it is how cheap it is to disagree with. An assistant you cannot cleanly reject is one you have to supervise, and supervising it costs more than doing the work.
how_we_build.pull: The model is the easy part. Everything around it is the editor.
how_we_build.hands_p1: While a long operation runs you keep working, so the document has two authors. The naive version of this loses an edit: the slower writer saves last and quietly overwrites what the other one did.
how_we_build.hands_p2: Every save is a compare-and-swap against the document's current head operation. A write built on a version that has moved is refused, not merged and not silently applied. Refusing is the useful behaviour — a rejected save can be retried against the truth, while a lost edit is discovered days later by the person who made it.
how_we_build.h2_once: Exactly once, or not at all
how_we_build.once_p1: A step of an assistant plan will eventually meet a retry, a double click, a lost connection, a refresh, a crash halfway, or two executors that both believe they own it. Any of those can apply an edit twice, and an edit applied twice to a timeline is not a duplicate — it is a different timeline.
how_we_build.once_p2: So the executor is not allowed to decide. Before it changes anything it has to claim the step from the plan store, which grants it atomically under a lock; only a granted claim authorises the edit, and a replay returns the first result without touching the document. What proves an operation happened is a recorded operation id, not a flag in a browser tab.
how_we_build.h2_models: The models sit beside the timeline, not behind an upload
how_we_build.models_p1: Matting, segmentation and depth run in the same process as the editor, on the frames it already has in hand. There is no export, no upload, no waiting, no re-import, and nothing to line back up afterwards.
how_we_build.models_p2: That is a design choice about latency, and it settles a question the seam usually leaves open: footage under embargo stays under embargo, because it never left. Where work genuinely needs the cloud it goes through one gateway that meters it against the account that asked for it.
how_we_build.h2_parity: A preview close enough to approve
how_we_build.parity_p1: The scrub and the final render come off the same timeline, and the colour maths of the export is a deliberate port of the preview's, so what you approve is what you ship everywhere except transitions. That exception is real and we would rather name it here than let you find it in a delivery: the export runs none of the preview's transition shaders. It hands them to the encoder's own set, where about ten of ours have a match by name and the rest are approximated — and a transition drops to a plain cross-dissolve whenever the clips either side cannot be handed over intact, which includes reversed footage, variable speed, per-clip fades, drop shadows, blend modes, keyframed geometry, and the second of two transitions placed back to back. Everything that is not a transition renders from the same description in both. Without that, every AI edit would be provisional: you would be accepting a picture and re-checking the file later, which is the seam reappearing at the other end of the pipeline.
how_we_build.parity_p2: Taken together — one document, one set of operations, one undo, one head, one execution, one colour pipeline — the interesting question stops being how good the model is. It becomes how cheaply you can disagree with it. That is the part we build.

shape.doc_v: One per project; operations are the only way in
shape.ops_v: Emits the editor's own operations, not code
shape.once_v: Claimed from the plan store, replay-safe
shape.models_v: In process, on the frames already loaded

how_we_build.rail_cost_body: Routing an assistant through the editor's own operations means it can only do what the editor can do. A model that could write arbitrary code would be more capable and much harder to undo, review or trust. That was the trade, and it was made deliberately.

about.title: A technology company that ships — Spinne Software
about.description: Why Spinne Software builds its own products rather than taking contracts, how the work is decided, and the diligence answers — including the ones that are no.
about.og_description: Own products rather than contracts, so the engineering compounds and the decisions stay here. How the work is decided, and the diligence answers.
about.tw_description: An Italian software company building its own products. What it is for, how it decides, and the exact compliance position.
about.lede: Spinne Software makes its own software instead of taking contracts. It is one engineer in Rome, and the order of the work is deliberate: build the machinery once, then build the products that stand on it. The ambition is stated plainly — products that hold their own against the best in their category, built by a company small enough to finish them.
about.why_p1: Contract work pays for someone else's roadmap. Owning the product means the engineering compounds instead of being handed over — every system Sparkle needed, the next thing inherits.
about.why_p2: It also means the decisions stay here. What gets built next is settled by what the work needs rather than by whichever customer is largest this quarter, and the parts that decide what the product can become are owned rather than rented; the ones we rent are named further down this page.
about.pull: Independence is not a preference. It is the difference between choosing and being told.
about.h2_one: One engineer, and what that buys
about.one_p1: Nothing is lost in translation between the person who decided something and the person who built it, and every part of the system still has an author who can explain why it is the way it is. What it costs is parallelism: one thing at a time, finished.
about.decided_p1: A feature starts from something a person cannot do today, not from a model that was released last week. The technology is chosen after the problem, which is why some of it runs on the machine in front of you, some of it runs in a data centre, and some of it was left out because the honest version did not work yet.
about.decided_p2: What is wrong gets fixed rather than documented. A defect is not a known limitation, and a design that only holds if the user is careful is a design that does not hold.
about.built_p1: — a desktop video editor with GPU rendering, local AI for matting, segmentation and depth, hardware encoding across four vendor stacks, and the team accounts, per-member subscriptions, metered credits and Italian electronic invoicing that a product of that size cannot ship without. In private preview at
about.compliance_intro: Diligence questions arrive eventually, so here are the answers in advance, including the ones that are no.

compliance.head: Security controls: implemented, not audited.
compliance.body: Role-based access, tenant isolation with tests that prove it, append-only audit logs, second-person approval on sensitive administrative actions, GDPR retention and erasure across the schema, credential rotation with recorded evidence. All built, and we will walk anyone through any of it. There is no SOC 2 attestation and no ISO/IEC 27001 certificate.

compliance.head: Card data never reaches us.
compliance.body: Payments go through Stripe. No card number touches a system we operate.

compliance.head: On GDPR we build the mechanism; a controller writes the policy.
compliance.body: Retention and erasure implemented in the schema rather than described in a document.

compliance.head: We build on
compliance.body: Claude, GPT-5 and Gemini for the assistant; Google Veo, Kling, MiniMax Hailuo and Luma Ray for video; Nano Banana, FLUX, Seedream and Ideogram for images; ElevenLabs for voice, sound and dubbing; Suno for music; Topaz for restoration. They are reached through fal.ai, OpenRouter, AI/ML API and Higgsfield; payments run through Stripe, and speech to text through Deepgram and Google Cloud. Integration only — not a partnership, endorsement or affiliation.

about.details_note: Published so they can be checked. An Italian counterparty can look the registration up in the Registro Imprese, and probably should.
about.talking_p1: Investors, partners, suppliers and press are welcome to write. A specific question gets a specific answer, usually within a working day.
about.rail_name_body: Spinne is German for spider. A web is one structure made of many threads, each doing a specific job, and it is repaired rather than rebuilt.

The only data anyone receives when you read a page is the handful of technical details every web server needs in order to send it to you. They are described in full below.

answers_transcribe.title: Transcribing video without uploading it — Spinne Software
answers_transcribe.description: Whisper runs on your machine. Which Sparkle setting keeps the audio there, why Auto does not, and what the eight-minute threshold actually decides.
answers_transcribe.og_description: Naming a local Whisper model keeps the audio on your machine. Auto sends it to a cloud engine at any length. The difference, and where it lives in the code.
answers_transcribe.tw_description: Which Sparkle settings keep audio on your machine, and the one that does not.
answers_transcribe.lede: Whisper runs on your own machine. Getting from that to a subtitle file on a timeline is the part nobody writes down — and the part where footage quietly leaves the building.
answers_transcribe.short_a: Name a Whisper model — tiny, base, small, medium or large-v3-turbo — and the audio never leaves your machine. Not “is encrypted in transit”. Does not leave.
answers_transcribe.short_b: Leave the engine on Auto and the answer changes, which is the next section.
answers_transcribe.short_p: Sparkle ships two local speech engines: whisper.cpp by preference, faster-whisper when it is not available. Both run locally, in the application's own backend. On Apple Silicon the bulk of the work is already on the Metal GPU.
answers_transcribe.h2_auto: When Auto does upload, and why
answers_transcribe.auto_warn_a: Auto is not local-first at any length. With a cloud engine configured, Auto sends the audio to it — Deepgram first, Google Cloud second — however short the file. Local Whisper is what Auto falls back to when no cloud engine is configured, or when every one of them fails.
answers_transcribe.auto_warn_b: The eight-minute threshold is not the local-versus-cloud gate. Past 480 seconds, measured with ffprobe before anything is sent, the request is pinned to Deepgram and Google drops out of the chain.
answers_transcribe.auto_p1: The reason for that threshold is the older Google engine, which caps out at roughly eight minutes of audio and was never a candidate for long files. It decides which cloud engine, not whether the cloud is used at all.
answers_transcribe.auto_p2: The fallback runs one way only, and it is worth being precise about it, because it is the whole promise:
auto_rules: A named local model never becomes a cloud call. The branch that talks to a cloud engine is entered only when the requested engine is a cloud engine, or is Auto. A request for small cannot reach it.
A cloud engine falls back to local. If Deepgram is unconfigured, unhealthy, or fails mid-job, the work lands on local Whisper rather than failing.
answers_transcribe.auto_p3: So the setting is the whole control surface. If footage is under embargo or covered by an NDA, name the model. Do not leave it on Auto and hope.
answers_transcribe.model_p1: On Auto, when it does stay local, the priority is the largest model that will run: large-v3-turbo, then medium, small, base, tiny. Naming one explicitly overrides that.
answers_transcribe.model_p2: There is no VRAM floor to clear. Sparkle does not refuse to run on a machine; it takes what the machine has and degrades. The practical limit is patience, not hardware.
answers_transcribe.model_p3: One detail that costs people a hot laptop elsewhere: transcription threads are capped to the performance cores, roughly half the logical count and never more than eight. Saturating the efficiency cores too bought almost nothing — the heavy lifting on Apple Silicon is already on the GPU — and cooked the machine for it.
answers_transcribe.h2_local: What else runs locally, and what it weighs
answers_transcribe.local_p1: Transcription is not the only model Sparkle runs locally. The largest of them, by file size:
local_models: Segment Anything ViT-B — subject segmentation — 358 MB
Segment Anything 2.1, Hiera-small — mask tracking — 176 MB
Robust Video Matting, ResNet-50 — background removal, quality — 103 MB
MobileSAM checkpoint — segmentation, fast path — 39 MB
MobileSAM encoder — segmentation, fast path — 27 MB
SAM ViT-H decoder — segmentation, decode — 16 MB
Robust Video Matting, MobileNetV3 — background removal, fast — 14 MB
answers_transcribe.local_total: None of these weights are inside the download. The application keeps its models in its own data folder, separately from the installer, which is why the sizes above are not what you fetch when you install it.
answers_transcribe.h2_accel: The neural accelerator is not always the fast path
answers_transcribe.accel_p1: This is the part that surprises people, and it is measured rather than assumed. On Apple Silicon, Sparkle deliberately runs background removal on the CPU and demotes CoreML below it:
accel_rows: RVM ResNet-50 — CPU ~76 ms/frame against CoreML ~150 ms/frame, twice as slow.
RVM MobileNetV3 — CPU ~43 ms/frame against CoreML ~104 ms/frame, 2.4 times as slow.
answers_transcribe.accel_p2: The cause is specific. The matting model carries recurrent state across frames and takes a float downsample_ratio input. The CoreML execution provider cannot run those, so it partitions the graph and hands the unsupported nodes back to the CPU one at a time, paying a copy between providers at every transition. The copies cost more than the acceleration saves.
answers_transcribe.accel_p3: CUDA and DirectML are real accelerators for this model and stay at the top of the order. CoreML sits below plain CPU as a last resort, for the case where the CPU provider is somehow absent. Measured on an M-series machine with ONNX Runtime 1.26.
not_items: Auto will not keep audio local, at any length. If a cloud engine is configured, Auto uses it. Name a model if that matters.

Mask tracking through SAM is not offered on Auto. Measured at 27 to 40 seconds per frame on an M2, it is too slow to hand to somebody without warning, so it is excluded from automatic selection rather than quietly chosen. The optical-flow tracking that ships in the editor is a different path and is not affected.
